title: Quadrilaterals & Polygons
coreInsight: Polygons belong to nested families defined by properties, and their angle structure can often be understood by decomposing them into triangles.
targetLearnerRealization: Polygon names encode properties that can overlap, while triangulation and boundary turns expose angle structure independent of appearance.
learningObjectives: Classify quadrilaterals using stated side, angle, and parallel-line properties.
Recognize nested categories such as square, rectangle, and rhombus.
Derive an n-gon's interior-angle sum from n−2 triangles.
Define regular polygons through equal sides and equal angles.
Use a consistent exterior turn and account for internal shared edges.

continuity.openingCallback: Use side equality, parallelism, and right angles as constraints that remain meaningful when a figure rotates or changes pose.
closingSeeds: Polygon boundaries can be transformed while angles, lengths, or orientation change in controlled ways.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: Shape categories are mutually exclusive, so a square is not also a rectangle.
A polygon's name determines properties not stated or implied.
A regular polygon is just any many-sided polygon.
Interior and exterior angles can be mixed without defining the turn.

beats.purpose: Break mutually exclusive shape-category thinking before formal hierarchy language.
beats.expectedRealization: A square satisfies the definitions of rectangle, rhombus, parallelogram, and quadrilateral simultaneously.
beats.transitionIn: Equal sides and equal angles classified triangles even when they rotated. Apply the same property-first habit to four-sided figures.
beats.whyNow: A square is the cleanest counterexample to single-label classification.
beats.entryBridge: Test each definition against the square's actual properties.
beats.exitBridge: One figure can satisfy several nested definitions at once.
learnerPrompts: Which list contains only categories that every square belongs to?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. A square is a rectangle, rhombus, parallelogram, and quadrilateral.
beats.incorrectFeedback: A rectangle needs four right angles; a rhombus needs four equal sides. A square has both.

visual.ariaLabel: Square properties supporting four nested quadrilateral classifications

steps.body: Definitions can overlap. Extra properties place a figure in a more specific family without removing broader memberships.

resolution.takeaway: Shape families are nested, not mutually exclusive.

beats.purpose: Classify from sufficient properties while refusing unstated ones.
beats.expectedRealization: Two pairs of parallel opposite sides guarantee a parallelogram, but not right angles or equal sides.
beats.transitionIn: Remove the square's right-angle and equal-side badges while keeping both opposite pairs parallel.
beats.prompt: A quadrilateral has both pairs of opposite sides parallel. What classification is guaranteed?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Parallel opposite pairs define a parallelogram; stronger names need more facts.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Do not import right angles or equal-side marks that were not given.

steps.body: The parallel-pair condition is sufficient for parallelogram. It permits, but does not force, rectangle, rhombus, or square properties.

resolution.takeaway: Use every stated property—and no invented ones.

beats.purpose: Derive polygon interior sums from non-overlapping triangles.
beats.expectedRealization: Diagonals from one vertex partition a convex n-gon into n−2 triangles.
beats.transitionIn: A quadrilateral can be split by one diagonal into two triangles. Continue the fan from one vertex of a hexagon.
beats.prompt: How many non-overlapping triangles are formed by drawing diagonals from one vertex of a convex hexagon?
beats.correctFeedback: Yes. A six-sided polygon fans into 6−2=4 triangles.
beats.incorrectFeedback: The chosen vertex connects to every non-neighboring vertex; count the resulting regions, not diagonals.

steps.title: Count the fan
steps.body: Four triangles cover the hexagon without overlap, so its interior angles total 4×180°=720°.

beats.purpose: Define regularity through both equal sides and equal angles.
beats.expectedRealization: Equilateral alone or equiangular alone is insufficient in general polygon language.
beats.transitionIn: The angle-sum total belongs to every hexagon. Equal sharing requires extra structure.
beats.prompt: Which condition makes a polygon regular?

options.text: All sides equal and all interior angles equal

beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Regular means both equilateral and equiangular.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Regularity controls both side lengths and angle measures.

steps.body: For a regular n-gon, each interior angle is ((n−2)×180°)/n because the total is shared equally.

resolution.takeaway: Regular polygons have equal sides and equal angles.

beats.purpose: Separate exterior turns from interior angles and derive their full-turn sum.
beats.expectedRealization: Taking one same-direction exterior turn at each vertex completes exactly 360° around any convex polygon.
beats.transitionIn: Walk the polygon boundary instead of triangulating its interior. At every vertex, turn just enough to follow the next side.
beats.prompt: Walking once around a convex polygon and always turning in the same direction, what is the sum of those exterior turns?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Your direction makes one complete 360° rotation.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Track the direction you face: after one circuit it has completed one full turn.

steps.body: Each exterior turn supplements its interior angle, but the clean invariant is directional: all same-direction turns total 360°.

resolution.takeaway: Define exterior angles as consistent boundary turns before adding them.

beats.purpose: Name nested families, regularity, and angle formulas after construction.
beats.expectedRealization: Definitions and decompositions—not names alone—justify polygon claims.
beats.name: Polygon properties and angle structure
beats.conciseDefinition: Polygon families may nest when one figure satisfies several definitions. A convex n-gon fans into n−2 triangles; a regular polygon shares its angle total equally; one circuit of exterior turns totals 360°.
beats.formalization: interior sum=(n−2)180° · regular interior=((n−2)180°)/n · exterior-turn sum=360°
beats.memoryHook: Properties classify; triangles total; boundary turns once.

beats.purpose: Transfer polygon properties and decomposition to a composite outer boundary.
beats.expectedRealization: Adding all component sides counts each glued edge twice even though neither copy remains outside.
beats.transitionIn: A polygon's side count describes its boundary. Glue regular polygons together and distinguish internal shared edges from the resulting outer boundary.
beats.whyNow: The learner can reason from definitions and exact coverage, so the composite chain tests boundary accounting rather than visual counting.
beats.entryBridge: Add every component side, count the five glued joins, and remove both copies of each shared edge.
beats.exitBridge: Thirty-three raw sides minus ten internal copies leaves twenty-three outer sides.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Polygon outlines with defining properties and boundary edges highlighted.
learnerPrompts: Which regular polygons appear in the chain?
How many sides are counted before gluing?
Why does each glued edge remove two counted sides?
Which edges actually lie on the outside boundary?
beats.incorrectFeedback: There are six polygons and five joins; each join hides one side from each neighbor.

steps.title: Remove internal copies
steps.body: Five glued edges each contributed two side counts, so subtract 2×5=10.

resolution.takeaway: Composite boundaries require subtracting internal shared edges from every shape that counted them.

beats.whyNow: Return to definitions after the composite construction.
beats.exitBridge: A rhombus is always a parallelogram but need not be a rectangle.
learnerPrompts: Which properties follow from four equal sides and opposite parallel pairs?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Every rhombus is a parallelogram.
beats.incorrectFeedback: A rhombus has both opposite pairs parallel; right angles are not required.

steps.body: The parallel-side property guarantees parallelogram membership. Without right angles, rectangle membership is not guaranteed.

resolution.takeaway: Broader families survive when extra properties are removed.

beats.purpose: Assess refusal to invent polygon properties.
beats.whyNow: Make insufficient information the correct mathematical conclusion.
beats.entryBridge: Separate the word quadrilateral from stronger subclasses.
beats.exitBridge: Four sides alone do not determine parallelism.
learnerPrompts: What does the name quadrilateral guarantee—and nothing more?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Parallel sides cannot be determined.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Quadrilateral guarantees exactly four sides, not any parallel pair.

steps.body: Some quadrilaterals have two parallel pairs, some one, and some none. No stronger fact is given.

resolution.takeaway: A category name grants only its defining properties.

beats.whyNow: Apply n−2 to a new side count.
beats.entryBridge: Count triangles from one vertex before multiplying by 180°.
beats.exitBridge: A nonagon gives seven triangles and 1260°.
learnerPrompts: How many triangles cover a nine-sided polygon?

beats.purpose: Assess equal sharing in a regular polygon.
beats.whyNow: Combine regularity with the derived sum.
beats.entryBridge: Find the octagon total, then divide equally among eight vertices.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Regularity makes all eight interior angles equal.

resolution.takeaway: Regularity turns a total into equal individual angles.

beats.purpose: Assess regular exterior turns without mixing angle types.
beats.exitBridge: A regular 15-gon turns 24° at each vertex.
beats.incorrectFeedback: A regular polygon shares the 360° exterior-turn total equally among 15 vertices.

steps.body: 360°/15=24°. The supplementary interior angle would be 156°, a different quantity.

resolution.takeaway: Name interior or exterior before calculating.

beats.purpose: Consolidate property, hierarchy, triangulation, and boundary reasoning.
beats.expectedRealization: Definitions determine classification; decomposition determines totals.
beats.transitionIn: Squares, parallelograms, hexagons, regular polygons, and glued chains all became precise once properties and boundaries were made explicit.
beats.prompt: Which actions belong in a reliable polygon routine? Select all four.

options.text: List only stated or implied properties.
Allow one figure to belong to several nested families.
Use n−2 non-overlapping triangles for interior sums.
Define a consistent exterior turn or outer boundary before counting.

response.feedback: Each action protects a different polygon claim.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes. Classify by properties and calculate through a justified decomposition or turn.
beats.incorrectFeedback: All four prevent prototype, naming, or angle-type errors.

steps.body: A polygon name is a compact property statement. When measurements are needed, triangulate the interior or walk the boundary deliberately.

resolution.takeaway: Properties classify; decompositions and turns calculate.

beats.purpose: Create a bridge to transformations without declaring a formal successor.
beats.expectedRealization: Moving a whole polygon can preserve some defining properties while changing its position or orientation.
beats.transitionIn: The categories survived rotations and the angle totals survived many shapes.
beats.prompt: If a polygon is slid, turned, reflected, or enlarged, which properties would you test to decide whether its family name still applies?
beats.takeaway: Track lengths, angles, parallel lines, orientation, and scale separately when a figure moves.

notes: Design: the square opens nested family membership, then property removal limits guaranteed classifications. A fan triangulation derives interior sums, regularity authorizes equal sharing, and a boundary walk derives the 360-degree exterior total. The authentic chain tests internal versus external edges.

Beat outline: nested-square anchor -> property guarantees -> triangulation -> regularity -> exterior turns -> name -> authentic polygon chain -> five independent problems -> consolidation -> transformation hook.
